<meta>continues from previous page</meta> shines with piety, religion, prudence, and the worship and veneration of God, as if seen through the eyes of true reason. By the confidence of his belief, he excels among men as much as the sun outshines the other stars by its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its power as by its divinity and holiness. Believe that this sun, O Asclepius, is second to God, governing all other things and illuminating all worldly beings, whether they are animate or inanimate. For if the world is a living being <note>original: "animal mundus," referring to the concept of the Anima Mundi or World Soul</note>, always living, and has been, and is, and shall be, nothing in the world is mortal. Since every single part of a living being, which exists in the world as in one and the same ever-living animal, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him to live forever. 

Therefore, just as the world is sempiternal, so is the sun itself always the governor of vital things, or rather the fosterer and dispenser of their entire liveliness. God is thus the sempiternal governor of the living beings, or the vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He has dispensed this life once by an eternal law, providing life to all vital beings in this manner which I shall describe.

<summary>Hermes explains to Asclepius that the pious man excels among others like the sun among stars. He describes the world as an eternally living being governed by the sun, which acts as the eternal dispenser of life under God's law.</summary>
<keywords>piety, sun, Asclepius, World Soul, immortality, eternal law, divinity, governor of life, vital beings</keywords>
